blocks.text: At a Turkmen wedding or festival, sooner or later a circle of people forms around two wrestlers. *Göreş*, Turkmen belt wrestling, is one of the oldest entertainments of the region; the same word, in local forms, names folk wrestling across the Turkic world. Each wrestler wears a belt or sash, a *guşak*, and grips his opponent's. The aim is to bring the other man down: in the usual rule, a wrestler loses when any part of his body other than his feet touches the ground. A wrestler interviewed by Euronews linked that rule to an old idea of honour: a Turkmen should never kneel before a rival.

A wrestler is a *pälwan*, a word that also means a champion or a strong man. At weddings, the hosts offered the prizes. Euronews mentions a horse or a camel for the winner; an account of the Turkmens of Iran describes a cow for the champion, a sheep for the runner-up and smaller gifts for the rest. Today göreş is also a modern sport, with weight classes, uniforms and world championships in belt wrestling, where Turkmen wrestlers regularly win medals. Women compete too: a Turkmen coach told Euronews that women began entering international tournaments in 2013.

Horse races belong to the same celebrations. At weddings, riders raced across open ground for prizes too; the account of the Turkmens of Iran describes straight races of three or four kilometres, a prize for the first rider to reach the groom's house, and riders who start training at about five. In Turkmenistan today, Akhal-Teke horses, the breed you met in [A1 unit 2](a1-u02-culture), race at the hippodrome near Ashgabat and in the regions, in a spring season and an autumn one. A race day usually has several races over different distances: one meeting in Mary in 2025 had seven, the second of them over 1,200 metres.

The last Sunday of April is the Day of the Turkmen Horse, a national holiday with races, a beauty contest for horses and an international fair. And at village weddings, wrestling and horse races still go together.

blocks.title: Can you ride?
blocks.text: To ride a horse is *ata münmek*, with *at* (horse) in the dative: *Ata münüp bilýärsiňmi?*, can you ride a horse? Remember the short *a*: *ata*, not *ada*, which is the dative of *at* with a long *a*, **name**.
With this unit's grammar, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Ertir obada toý bar. Toýda göreş bolar, atlar hem ýaryşar. Meniň doganym Batyr pälwan, ol gaty güýçli. Men göreşip bilmeýärin, ýöne ata münüp bilýärin. Belki men hem ýaryşaryn!
blocks.en: Tomorrow there's a wedding in the village. There will be wrestling at the wedding, and the horses will race too. My brother Batyr is a wrestler; he's very strong. I can't wrestle, but I can ride a horse. Maybe I'll race too!

questions.q: In göreş, when does a wrestler usually lose?
options: when any part of his body but his feet touches the ground
when he lets go of the belt
questions.explain: Touching the ground with anything but the feet loses the bout.
The belt is a *guşak*; the horse, *at*.

questions.q: In the reading, what can the writer do?
questions.explain: *Men göreşip bilmeýärin, ýöne ata münüp bilýärin*: I can't wrestle, but I can ride a horse.
